content: Hexosaminidase A, also referred to as HEXA, is an enzyme encoded by the HEXA gene, which is located on chromosome 15 in humans. This enzyme, along with the GM2 activator protein, plays a critical role in breaking down GM2 gangliosides and other molecules that contain terminal N-acetyl hexosamines. Hexosaminidase A is a heterodimer, meaning it is composed of two different subunits: an alpha subunit and a beta subunit. The alpha subunit is encoded by the HEXA gene, while the beta subunit is encoded by the HEXB gene. Mutations in the HEXB gene, which encodes the beta subunit, are associated with Sandhoff disease. In contrast, mutations in the HEXA gene, which encodes the alpha subunit, impair the hydrolysis of GM2 gangliosides, leading to Tay–Sachs disease. Although both the alpha and beta subunits of hexosaminidase A can cleave GalNAc residues, only the alpha subunit has the ability to hydrolyze GM2 gangliosides. This unique function of the alpha subunit is due to the presence of a critical residue, arginine at position 424 (Arg-424), which is essential for binding the N-acetyl-neuraminic acid residue of GM2 gangliosides. Additionally, the alpha subunit contains a specific loop structure formed by the amino acids glycine-280, serine-281, glutamic acid-282, and proline-283. This loop is absent in the beta subunit but is crucial for the binding of the GM2 activator protein (GM2AP) to the alpha subunit. The combination of Arg-424 and the loop structure enables the alpha subunit to hydrolyze GM2 gangliosides into GM3 gangliosides by removing the N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc) residue from GM2 gangliosides. Tay–Sachs disease is caused by a deficiency in hexosaminidase A, which results from various mutations in the HEXA gene. These mutations include gene deletions, nonsense mutations, and missense mutations. In individuals with Tay–Sachs disease, the enzyme loses its ability to remove the GalNAc residue from GM2 gangliosides. Consequently, GM2 gangliosides accumulate in the brain at levels 100 to 1000 times higher than normal. Over 100 different mutations have been identified in infantile cases of Tay–Sachs disease alone. The most common mutation, found in over 80% of patients, involves a four-base-pair insertion (TATC) in exon 11 of the HEXA gene. This insertion leads to the formation of a premature stop codon, resulting in a deficiency of hexosaminidase A. Children with Tay–Sachs disease typically die between the ages of two and six due to complications such as aspiration and pneumonia. The disease causes progressive cerebral degeneration, blindness, flaccid extremities, and seizures. Currently, there is no cure for Tay–Sachs disease. The HEXA gene encodes the lysosomal enzyme beta-hexosaminidase, which, in conjunction with the GM2 activator protein, is responsible for degrading GM2 gangliosides within lysosomes. Mutations in the HEXA gene disrupt this process, leading to the accumulation of toxic substances in the cells of the brain and spinal cord. This accumulation results in the fatal genetic disorder known as Tay–Sachs disease. Since the defect primarily affects neural cells, individuals with a HEXA mutation experience rapid deterioration of motor and cognitive functions, typically leading to death by the age of three or four. A genetically modified mouse model, known as a knockout model, has been used to study the effects of HEXA gene inactivation. Mice with the HEXA gene inactivated exhibit many of the same symptoms as human Tay–Sachs patients, with one notable difference: the distribution of GM2 ganglioside accumulation in the brain differs between the mice and human patients. This model has been instrumental in advancing research into gene therapies for HEXA mutations. In one study, researchers successfully restored beta-hexosaminidase levels and eliminated toxic cellular buildup in mice by using a non-replicating Herpes simplex virus vector to deliver the missing HEXA gene.
